summary.text: A critical point is the end point of a phase equilibrium curve; the best known and most studied is the liquid–vapor critical point.
At the critical temperature and pressure the phase boundary vanishes, and above it the substance is a supercritical fluid that pressure alone cannot turn into a liquid.
Close to the point the liquid and vapor become very similar and their properties change sharply; water turns compressible and becomes a poor solvent for salts.

facts.label: Discovered by
facts.value: Charles Cagniard de la Tour, in 1822

facts.label: Named by
facts.value: Mendeleev in 1860 and Thomas Andrews in 1869

facts.label: Carbon dioxide test
facts.value: Liquefied at 31 °C, but not slightly hotter even at 3000 atm

facts.label: Beyond the point
facts.value: A supercritical fluid, joined smoothly to liquid and gas

items.prompt: A gas is kept hotter than its critical temperature and squeezed harder and harder. What happens?

options.label: It turns to liquid once the pressure is high enough
It stays a fluid and never condenses into a liquid
It freezes directly into a solid at moderate pressure
It turns into a plasma at the critical pressure

items.explain: Above the critical temperature the substance is supercritical and cannot be liquefied by pressure alone; Cagniard found CO₂ would not liquefy slightly above 31 °C even at very high pressure.

items.prompt: On a pressure-temperature chart, you follow the line between liquid and vapor toward higher and higher temperatures. What eventually happens to it?

options.label: It stops at a point beyond which no boundary exists
It continues forever, with boiling at ever higher temperatures
It bends back and meets the line for the solid
It splits into two separate boundary lines

items.explain: The liquid-vapor boundary terminates at a critical point; beyond it the phase boundary vanishes.

items.prompt: Ordinary water is an excellent solvent for dissolved salts. What happens to that ability close to water's critical point?

options.label: It grows stronger as the water gets hotter
It stays about the same as at room conditions
It only works for gases and oils from then on
It becomes poor, the reverse of normal behavior

items.explain: Near the critical point water's properties flip: it becomes a bad solvent for electrolytes and mixes more readily with nonpolar gases and organic molecules.

items.prompt: A blended mixture of polymer and solvent is cooled and, past a certain threshold, splits into two liquid layers. If that is the hottest point where cooling causes the split, what is it called?

options.label: The lower critical solution temperature
The upper critical solution temperature
The Curie temperature
The triple point of the mixture

items.explain: The UCST is the hottest point at which cooling induces phase separation; the LCST is the coldest point at which heating does.

items.prompt: A magnet loses its magnetism when heated past its Curie temperature, with no outside magnetic field. How does thermodynamics classify this?

options.label: As another example of a critical point
As a triple point of the magnet
As a boiling point of the metal
As a supercritical fluid forming

items.explain: The ferromagnet-paramagnet transition at the Curie temperature without an external field is listed as an example of a critical point.

items.prompt: A student uses the van der Waals equation to predict how a fluid behaves right at its critical point. What goes wrong?

options.label: It predicts that no critical point exists at all
It works only for solids and not for fluids
It rests on a mean-field idea and gets the scaling laws wrong
It only holds for temperatures far below freezing

items.explain: The van der Waals equation is based on mean-field theory, which does not hold near the critical point and predicts wrong scaling laws.
